title: What If You Turned a Building Around With 600 People Working Inside?

scenes.text: What if you spun an office building around while everyone kept working? In 1930, Indianapolis did.
Indiana Bell needed a bigger headquarters, but its eight-story telephone exchange stood in the way.
So crews lifted all 11,000 tons onto rollers and pushed with jacks. Fifteen inches an hour.
Phone lines, gas, water and power were given slack and stayed connected. Staff came and went over a sidewalk that moved with the building.
In about a month it shifted over and turned a full 90 degrees. Six hundred people worked through it.
Service was never interrupted, and reportedly nobody inside felt it move. The architect's son was the novelist Kurt Vonnegut.

description:
What if you rotated an office building while everyone inside kept working? In the autumn of 1930 the Indiana Bell Telephone Company did exactly that in Indianapolis.
The eight-story, 11,000-ton exchange, built in 1907, was raised onto rollers and moved with jacks at about 15 inches an hour, shifted about 52 feet, turned 90 degrees and shifted again, all in roughly a month. Utility lines were lengthened and made flexible, a movable walkway kept the entrance open, and about 600 employees kept the telephone service running without an outage. The plan came from the architecture firm of Kurt Vonnegut Sr., father of the novelist. The building was demolished in 1963.
